opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is that they actually engage, because right now a lot of the conversation happens past each other. You have one group that's very focused on long-term, potentially catastrophic outcomes, and another group that's focused on harms happening today: bias, privacy, misuse, models failing for underrepresented languages and communities. Too often those get framed as competing for the same oxygen, the same funding, the same policy attention. I don't think that's a productive framing.

What I'd like to see is a recognition that a lot of the underlying technical problems are shared. If you care about whether a model will behave reliably in some far-future scenario, you should care deeply about why it fails today on a dialect it wasn't trained on, or why it memorizes and leaks data, or why we can't really explain what's happening inside it. Those are the same questions about robustness, interpretability, and control, just at different time horizons. The present-day failures are the empirical evidence we actually have.

Where I'd push the existential risk community is on grounding. Claims about risk should be tied to evidence and to measurable properties of systems, not just to speculation, because when the conversation becomes purely hypothetical it can crowd out harms that are concrete and documented. And policy built on very abstract scenarios can end up poorly calibrated, for instance using compute thresholds as a proxy for risk when the relationship between compute and capability or harm is a lot messier than people assume.

Where I'd push the responsible AI community is to not dismiss questions about where the technology is heading. These systems are changing quickly, and thinking ahead isn't inherently a distraction.

So practically: shared venues, shared benchmarks, and researchers who are willing to sit in rooms with people who prioritize differently. And a bit of humility on both sides, because frankly none of us has a great track record of predicting how this technology unfolds. The best thing we can do is build the scientific tools to understand these models better, and that benefits everyone regardless of which risks keep you up at night.

r001.rationale: The response says the two communities share technical questions and that present-day failures provide empirical evidence, but it does not say that research by many existential-risk researchers addresses current threat models.

r002.rationale: It mentions interpretability as a shared concern, but does not identify “mechanistic interpretability” and responsible-AI “interpretability” as different labels for the same concept.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and honestly my starting point is that the framing of these as two camps is itself part of the problem. I've spent most of my career on things like efficiency, interpretability, how compression and pruning change model behavior, and more recently on multilingual work and who gets left out of these systems. And what I keep noticing is that the questions that are supposedly "long-term" and the questions that are supposedly "near-term" are actually built on the same empirical foundations.

Take robustness. If you care about a model behaving in ways we didn't anticipate at some future scale, you have to care about the fact that right now, today, we don't have good tools for characterizing where a model fails. And the people who have been doing that work for years are often the people in the responsible AI community, looking at underrepresented groups, looking at the long tail of the data distribution, looking at how models memorize rare examples. Those aren't separate problems. The long tail is where both the fairness failures and the unpredictable behaviors live.

So my first answer is: engage through shared empirical questions, not through shared ideology. I don't think you need to agree on timelines or on how you'd weight a hypothetical catastrophe versus a documented harm happening to real people now. I actually think it's healthy to disagree about that. But you should be able to agree that we need better evaluation, that we need to understand how capabilities emerge with scale, that we need to understand what training data does to downstream behavior. Those are tractable research programs where the methods transfer across both communities.

The second thing I'd say, and I'll be a bit more pointed here, is that the existential risk community has to take seriously that attention and resources are finite, and that the way a problem gets framed shapes who gets to work on it. When the conversation becomes exclusively about frontier models at a handful of labs, it narrows the set of people who are seen as legitimate contributors. A lot of the most important safety-relevant work I've seen comes from people who would never describe themselves as safety researchers. They're working on low-resource languages, or on auditing, or on systems deployed in contexts the labs never thought about. If you're genuinely worried about how these systems go wrong, you want that breadth, not a monoculture of people who all read the same forums.

And the responsible AI community, to be fair, has sometimes been too quick to dismiss speculative concerns as distraction. I understand why. There's a real pattern of hypothetical harms getting more funding than documented ones. But dismissing a question because of who's asking it isn't a good scientific posture either. Some of the capability trends are genuinely surprising, and pretending they aren't doesn't help anyone.

So practically: co-locate at the same venues, build shared benchmarks, fund work that sits in the overlap, and be honest about disagreements rather than performing consensus. The worst outcome is two communities that each think they're the serious ones and spend their energy on that argument instead of on the actual science. We have a very short window to build the tools we'll need, and I'd rather spend it on the tools.

r002.rationale: It mentions interpretability as part of the speaker’s work, but does not identify mechanistic interpretability and responsible-AI interpretability as different labels for the same concept.

astra-6.text:
I think we need more dialogue between those communities, and a willingness to understand what each is worried about. Often the conversation gets framed as a choice: either you care about harms that are happening now, or you care about potentially catastrophic harms in the future. I don’t think that’s a useful divide.

But we do need to be precise about the claims we’re making. What are the assumptions behind a particular risk? What evidence would change our minds? And what can we do today that would help address it? Those questions give people a way to engage even when they disagree about timelines or probabilities.

There’s also common ground around understanding model behavior, evaluating failures, and making systems more accountable. I’d like to see more collaboration around concrete problems like those. You don’t need everyone to agree on the most important risk before you can do useful work together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need much more dialogue, and that starts with taking one another’s concerns seriously. There are real differences in what people think is likely, on what timescale, and what evidence they find persuasive. We should be able to discuss those differences without questioning whether someone cares about making AI safe.

One useful place to start is with concrete research questions. How do we evaluate systems? How do we understand their limitations? Who gets to decide what an acceptable risk is? Those questions can matter both to people concerned about harms today and to people concerned about future risks.

But collaboration doesn’t require collapsing everything into one agenda. We need room for different priorities, while being explicit about our assumptions and willing to change our minds. I’d like to see more conversations where the goal is to understand the disagreement and find useful work to do together.

r001.rationale: The response mentions concerns about harms today and future risks, but does not say that research by many existential-risk researchers addresses current threat models.
